name: Chennakeshava Temple, Belur
deity: Vishnu, worshipped as Chennakeshava (Vijayanarayana) — 'the handsome Keshava'
summary: On the banks of the Yagachi, King Vishnuvardhana raised this soapstone temple to Vishnu in 1117 — a building where every surface dissolves into sculpture and the celestial dancers of the bracket figures still seem mid-step after nine centuries.

sections.history: The Chennakeshava temple was consecrated in 1117 CE by the Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana, and later tradition ties its founding to his victory over the Cholas at Talakad. Whatever the immediate occasion, the temple announced the arrival of the Hoysalas as a great southern power and their dynastic devotion to Vishnu. Work did not stop with the founder: inscriptions record that the complex was elaborated over more than a century by his successors, so that Belur became a royal temple-town rather than a single shrine. Unlike many medieval monuments, worship here has never lapsed — the Chennakeshava is a living temple to this day, which is one reason UNESCO inscribed it, with its Hoysala sisters, as a World Heritage Site in 2023. Standing before it, a visitor sees at once why the Hoysala court prized artists so highly: several of the master sculptors signed their work, a rare medieval assertion of individual authorship.
sections.architecture: Belur is the temple that made the Hoysala manner famous. It is built not of granite but of chloritic schist — soapstone — which is soft enough to carve like ivory when freshly quarried and hardens on exposure, letting the sculptors work in astonishing depth and finish. The shrine stands on a raised star-shaped platform, the jagati, which the pilgrim circumambulates to read the temple's carved stories in sequence. Bands of friezes run around the base: elephants for stability, lions for courage, horsemen, and scrollwork, with epic scenes above. The pillars of the hall are each turned to a different design, some said to have been lathe-finished. Most celebrated of all are the madanikas, the bracket figures of celestial women beneath the eaves — a huntress, a dancer, a woman with a parrot — each a small masterpiece of poise. Where the imperial Cholas overwhelmed by scale, the Hoysalas astonish by intricacy.
sections.legends: The temple's presiding form, Chennakeshava, means the 'handsome' or 'beautiful' Keshava, an aspect of Vishnu, and devotees hold that Vishnuvardhana built it after his conversion under the Vaishnava teacher Ramanuja. A much-loved story attaches to the madanika bracket figures: the sculptor is said to have modelled one dancing figure on Queen Shantala Devi, herself a renowned dancer, so that the stone preserves not only a goddess-like ideal but the memory of a living queen. Another tradition surrounds the 'Darpana Sundari', the lady with the mirror, admired as the sculptors' study of grace itself. Such tales, whether history or devotion, express how completely the people of the region have taken these carvings to heart.
sections.festivals: As a living Vaishnava temple, Belur keeps a full ritual calendar. The great annual event is the car festival (rathotsava), when the processional image is drawn through the temple town in a decorated wooden ter to the pull of thousands of hands. Vaikuntha Ekadashi and the birthdays of Vishnu's forms bring special worship, and the temple observes the daily rhythm of offerings that has continued unbroken since Hoysala times. Because Chennakeshava remains consecrated — unlike its deconsecrated sister at Somanathapura — the visitor may witness the sculpture not as museum-pieces but as the setting of prayer still in use.
sections.experience: Belur rewards slowness. Arrive early, walk the star-shaped platform clockwise, and let the eye travel from the elephant frieze at your feet up through the running epics to the celestial dancers overhead — the temple is, in effect, a book that must be read on foot. Inside, the light is dim and the lathe-turned pillars gleam; a guide or a good eye will find the sculptors' signatures. The town is small and the neighbouring Shaiva temple of Halebidu lies a short drive away, so many pilgrims see the two on a single unhurried day in the Malnad foothills.

visit.timings: Open daily, roughly 7:30 am to 7:30 pm; worship is offered morning and evening. Early morning is coolest and least crowded.
visit.dressCode: Modest dress is expected in this living temple — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed before entering the shrine.
visit.photography: Photography of the exterior and its famed carvings is generally permitted; photography inside the sanctum is restricted. Follow posted signs and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Belur is in Hassan district, about 220 km west of Bengaluru and 40 km from Hassan town, which has the nearest railway station. Halebidu is around 16 km away, and the two are almost always visited together.
